es.summary: Alteración de la memoria y funciones ejecutivas que no interfiere significativamente con la vida diaria, pero aumenta el riesgo de progresión a demencia.
key_points: Es una condición intermedia entre el envejecimiento normal y la demencia.
No existen tratamientos farmacológicos probados; se manejan causas reversibles y se promueve el estilo de vida saludable.
Se requiere seguimiento cada 6‑12 meses para detectar progresión.
Los exámenes neuropsicológicos (p. ej., MMSE <27) y de imagen ayudan al diagnóstico.

pathophysiology: Pérdida progresiva de neuronas en áreas relacionadas con la memoria (hipocampo, corteza prefrontal).
Acumulación de beta‑amiloide y tau puede estar presente, pero sin suficiente daño para demencia.
Factores vasculares (hipertensión, diabetes) pueden contribuir a daño cerebral subcortical.
risk_factors: Historia familiar de demencia o enfermedad de Alzheimer.
Uso crónico de anticolinérgicos o sedantes.
signs_symptoms: Olvido frecuente de objetos o citas.
Desorientación ocasional en tiempo o lugar.
Mantiene la capacidad de realizar actividades de la vida diaria.
diagnostics: Evaluación clínica de historia y examen físico.
Imágenes cerebrales (TC o RM) para descartar lesiones estructurales.
Laboratorios básicos para excluir causas reversibles (TSH, B12, glucosa).
treatment: Control de factores de riesgo vascular (presión arterial, glucemia, lípidos).
Revisión y ajuste de medicación que pueda afectar la cognición.
Intervenciones no farmacológicas: entrenamiento cognitivo, ejercicio aeróbico, dieta mediterránea.
Apoyo psicosocial y educación al paciente y familia.
complications: Progresión a demencia mayor (Alzheimer, demencia vascular).
Aumento del riesgo de caídas y lesiones por desorientación.
Pérdida de autonomía y dependencia en actividades de la vida diaria.
nursing_care: Evaluar orientación, memoria y capacidad de juicio en cada turno.
Mantener ambiente seguro: eliminar obstáculos, usar señalización clara.
Registrar cambios en la función cognitiva y comunicar al equipo.
Facilitar rutinas estructuradas y recordatorios escritos.
patient_teaching: Uso de agendas, listas y alarmas para recordar citas y medicamentos.
Importancia de la actividad física regular y una dieta balanceada.
Evitar alcohol y sedantes que empeoren la cognición.
Programar visitas regulares al médico para monitoreo.

outcomes: Orientación: orientado a tiempo, lugar y persona en 80% de evaluaciones
Seguridad: sin episodios de caída relacionados con desorientación durante la estancia

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de orientación y registrar datos cada 4 horas
interventions.rationale: Permite detectar cambios tempranos y guiar intervenciones.

interventions.action: Revisar y ajustar medicación que pueda causar confusión
interventions.rationale: Reducir agentes anticolinérgicos o sedantes disminuye la alteración cognitiva.

interventions.action: Proveer un entorno bien iluminado y con señales visuales claras
interventions.rationale: Facilita la orientación y reduce la desorientación.

interventions.action: Instruir al paciente a usar una agenda o reloj con alarmas
interventions.rationale: Apoya la memoria y disminuye la confusión.

interventions.action: Mantener comunicación simple y repetir información clave
interventions.rationale: Mejora la comprensión y reduce la frustración.

outcomes: Incidencia de caídas: 0 durante el periodo de cuidado
Uso de dispositivos de seguridad (barandillas, calzado antideslizante) en 100% de los momentos

interventions.action: Realizar evaluación del entorno para identificar riesgos de tropiezo
interventions.rationale: Previene caídas al eliminar obstáculos.

interventions.action: Colocar barra de apoyo y tapetes antideslizantes en el baño
interventions.rationale: Reduce el riesgo de caída en áreas de alto riesgo.

interventions.action: Asegurar que el paciente use calzado cerrado y antideslizante
interventions.rationale: Mejora la estabilidad al caminar.

interventions.action: Programar asistencia al levantarse de la cama o silla
interventions.rationale: Previene caídas por pérdida de equilibrio al iniciar el movimiento.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de transferencia segura y uso de dispositivos de apoyo
interventions.rationale: Fomenta la autonomía segura.

en.summary: Alteration of memory and executive functions that does not significantly interfere with daily life, but increases the risk of progression to dementia.
key_points: It is an intermediate condition between normal aging and dementia.
No proven pharmacologic treatments; reversible causes are managed and a healthy lifestyle is promoted.
Follow-up every 6‑12 months is required to detect progression.
Neuropsychological tests (e.g., MMSE <27) and imaging aid diagnosis.

pathophysiology: Progressive loss of neurons in memory-related areas (hippocampus, prefrontal cortex).
Accumulation of beta‑amyloid and tau may be present, but not enough damage for dementia.
Vascular factors (hypertension, diabetes) can contribute to subcortical brain injury.
risk_factors: Family history of dementia or Alzheimer’s disease.
Chronic use of anticholinergics or sedatives.
signs_symptoms: Frequent forgetting of objects or appointments.
Occasional disorientation in time or place.
Maintains ability to perform activities of daily living.
diagnostics: Brain imaging (CT or MRI) to rule out structural lesions.
Basic labs to exclude reversible causes (TSH, B12, glucose).
treatment: Control of vascular risk factors (blood pressure, glucose, lipids).
Review and adjust medications that may affect cognition.
Non‑pharmacologic interventions: cognitive training, aerobic exercise, Mediterranean diet.
Psychosocial support and education for patient and family.
complications: Progression to major dementia (Alzheimer’s, vascular dementia).
Increased risk of falls and injuries due to disorientation.
Loss of autonomy and dependence in activities of daily living.
nursing_care: Assess orientation, memory, and judgment at each shift.
Maintain a safe environment: remove obstacles, use clear signage.
Document changes in cognitive function and communicate to the team.
Facilitate structured routines and written reminders.
patient_teaching: Use planners, lists, and alarms to remember appointments and medications.
Importance of regular physical activity and a balanced diet.
Avoid alcohol and sedatives that worsen cognition.
Schedule regular physician visits for monitoring.

outcomes: Orientation: oriented to time, place, and person in 80% of assessments
Safety: no falls related to disorientation during stay

interventions.action: Assess level of orientation and record data every 4 hours
interventions.rationale: Allows early detection of changes and guides interventions.

interventions.action: Review and adjust medications that may cause confusion
interventions.rationale: Reducing anticholinergics or sedatives decreases cognitive alteration.

interventions.action: Provide a well‑lit environment with clear visual cues
interventions.rationale: Facilitates orientation and reduces disorientation.

interventions.action: Instruct patient to use a planner or alarm clock
interventions.rationale: Supports memory and reduces confusion.

interventions.action: Maintain simple communication and repeat key information
interventions.rationale: Improves understanding and reduces frustration.

outcomes: Use of safety devices (handrails, non‑slip footwear) in 100% of occasions

interventions.action: Conduct environmental assessment to identify trip hazards
interventions.rationale: Prevents falls by removing obstacles.

interventions.action: Place grab bars and non‑slip mats in the bathroom
interventions.rationale: Reduces fall risk in high‑risk areas.

interventions.action: Ensure patient uses closed, non‑slip footwear
interventions.rationale: Improves stability when walking.

interventions.action: Schedule assistance when getting out of bed or chair
interventions.rationale: Prevents falls from loss of balance when initiating movement.

interventions.action: Teach patient safe transfer techniques and use of assistive devices
interventions.rationale: Promotes safe autonomy.

key_points.1.quote: At this time, there is no proven drug treatment for MCI.

key_points.2.quote: Because MCI may be an early sign of Alzheimer's disease , it's really important to see your health care provider every 6 to 12 months.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Medical experts have not identified the specific cause(s) of Alzheimer disease, but it appears to be linked to factors such as a family history of Alzheimer disease; poor lifestyle, such as lack of exercise and excessive alcohol consumption; head trauma; and environmental factors, such as excessive exposure to air pollution.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: MCI memory problems may include: Losing things often Forgetting to go to events and appointments Having more trouble coming up with words than other people of the same age

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: MCI memory problems may include: Losing things often Forgetting to go to events and appointments Having more trouble coming up with words than other people of the same age

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: People with MCI can take care of themselves and do their normal activities.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: Health-care professionals assess and diagnose MND with a physical examination that includes a review of the patient’s symptoms, as well as diagnostic tests.

sections.diagnostics.2.quote: In addition, MRIs provide evidence to rule out other conditions and diseases that have symptoms similar to Alzheimer disease, such as brain tumors and strokes.

sections.complications.0.quote: Insufficient blood and oxygen to the brain leading to damage to the brain’s blood vessels causes vascular dementia .
